transcript:
Header: 2025-10-07 15:30 PDT | Duration: 52m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO), Sofia Alvarez (ML Platform), Tom Reed (Infra)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. Quick intros—I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Liam is our SE who will do the parity plan.
[00:12] Raj: Hi, Raj here. We're trying to figure out whether to move more workloads off OpenAI and consolidate on something we can host or use Redwood dedicated. We're currently using OpenAI for convenience and a self-hosted vLLM/TGI path for latency-critical stuff.
[00:25] Liam: nice, got it. Can you briefly describe which endpoints are latency-critical and what your SLOs look like?
[00:31] Sofia: Sure, our vector search QA and realtime chat—targets are 90th percentile sub 120ms for short prompts (~128 tokens) and bursty trough to peak traffic. For longer document summarization we can tolerate higher latency.
[00:44] Tom: also cost is a driver. vLLM is cheaper per token but maintenance is painful and we see output differences between OpenAI and self-hosted models.
[00:52] Maya: that's helpful. Quick Q: when you say differences, is that in raw logits/determinism or function-calling and output shape?
[00:58] Sofia: a bit of both. Function calling behavior is inconsistent between OpenAI's function schema and our self-hosted TGI endpoints—sometimes the JSON blobs come back slightly malformed or missing fields, which breaks downstream parsers.
[01:12] Raj: and tokenization differences too — some prompts that match on OpenAI diverge in outputs on our vLLM runs. We need eval parity for our product's SLAs.
[01:22] Liam: okay, so three buckets I hear: API/format compatibility (function calling, streaming), model output parity (evals/golden responses), and infra/ops (latency, KV cache, batching). Does that capture it?
[01:30] Raj: yep.
[01:32] Maya: quick overview — Redwood offers hosted for quick onboarding, Dedicated for predictable capacity and isolation, and Private/VPC/on-prem for strict compliance. SE will walk through how we approach parity testing.
[01:44] Liam: sure. On the compatibility side—Redwood supports OpenAI-style endpoints and function call semantics; we also maintain model variants tuned for lower latency (quantized) and have streaming that chunks tokens similarly to OpenAI so your parsers should be reusable with minimal changes. There are subtle differences in tokenization across model families — we suggest running a tokenization normalization pass but we can also run direct output comparisons.
[02:07] Tom: do you support the same content filters and moderation hooks as OpenAI? We have compliance rules.
[02:12] Liam: yes, we have moderation options and you can opt to run content filters client-side or as a platform-level policy; for enterprise private deployments we integrate with your DLP too.
[02:21] Sofia: tangent—how does KV cache behave for sessions? Our chat service keeps a long context with incremental KV lookups. vLLM's cache hits are high and that helps latency.
[02:32] Liam: Redwood's runtime maintains KV caches per session and supports hot-warm memory tiers; cache eviction and prefix caching are tunable. In Dedicated you can pin instances for warm caches which helps burst behavior.
[02:44] Raj: benchmarking — what's the proposed approach? We have a 1k-prompt eval set with golden outputs, and a mix of microbenchmarks for tail latency.
[02:53] Liam: perfect. We'll run three experiments: 1) functional equivalence on the eval set comparing Redwood-hosted and your vLLM baseline (same model family where possible), 2) latency/cost benchmarks (tokens/sec, p50/p90/p99), 3) streaming & function-calling stress tests to catch parsing edge cases. We'll produce a delta report with examples where outputs diverge.
[03:13] Sofia: do you need our raw prompts or can we hash them? We have privacy constraints.
[03:18] Maya: we can accept hashed/hob-sanitized prompts, and for anything sensitive we can run the tests in your private deployment or under a dedicated tenancy with NDA.
[03:27] Raj: good. Another concern — quantization. We run int8 quantized models on vLLM and the outputs differ a bit. How do you handle quantized variants?
[03:37] Liam: Redwood supports multiple execution paths: float16, int8, experimental int4 in some cases. We annotate performance and quality profiles per model/quantization level. The parity run will include the quantized profile you use to measure drift.
[03:50] Tom: networking question — for Redwood Dedicated can we peer via AWS PrivateLink or do you need VPN?
[03:57] Liam: we support VPC peering, PrivateLink, and for Private deployments you get customer-controlled VPCs. We'll share a network diagram.
[04:05] Raj: security — SOC2 is must have. SSO/SAML and audit logs too. KMS for key management?
[04:11] Maya: yes to all. We'll attach our SOC2 report and a short security packet. KMS integrations (customer-managed keys) are available in Private and Dedicated with some caveats.
[04:22] Speaker 1: (inaudible) oh sorry that was me—
[04:26] Liam: another practical point — function calling schemas. If you have strict shapes, we recommend schema validation in your ingestion layer but we've found differences usually come from streaming chunks getting split in mid-json; we can enable chunk-aware emit that tag boundaries to make reassembly robust.
[04:44] Sofia: that's exactly the bug we hit — sometimes a function call JSON is split across two chunks and our parser fails.
[04:50] Liam: we can simulate that in stress tests and show mitigations.
[04:55] Raj: cost — if we move everything hosted to Redwood hosted, costs need to be comparable. How do you position hosted vs dedicated cost wise?
[05:02] Maya: hosted is OPEX with pay-as-you-go; Dedicated is for predictable throughput and better per-token economics at commit tiers. We'll share a comparison spreadsheet.
[05:10] Tom: for POC do you offer a dedicated short-term pool or reserved burst to match our peak?
[05:16] Liam: yes, we can provision a pilot Dedicated cluster for the benchmark window or run in Hosted with reserved capacity for the test. Pilot is flexible.
[05:24] Raj: timeline — we're hoping to decide by end of Q4, run pilots in October.
[05:29] Maya: that fits. Next steps: we'll send the pricing sheet, security docs, and Liam will draft the parity plan. We'll set the pilot kickoff for next week if you can confirm dates.
[05:40] Sofia: will do. Also please share any quickstart scripts for migrating existing vLLM config to Redwood runtime.
[05:46] Liam: yes — we have a migration repo and a checklist for model artifacts, quant configs, tokenizer mapping. I'll share links.
[05:54] Raj: great, thanks.

End of recording.

Shared links mentioned: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2.pdf , https://github.com/redwood-inference/migration-quickstart (demo only)

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels and word swaps, e.g., TGI sometimes transcribed as "T G I"; vLLM pronounced "vee LLM".
